title: Quickly extracting fidelity decay rates in random circuit benchmarking experiments
authors: Ake Köhne, Stavros Efthymiou, Joanna Majsak, Jadwiga Wilkens, Bram Evert, Andrew D. Patterson, Jonas Helsen, Markus Heinrich, Ingo Roth
abstract: Randomized benchmarking (RB) with structured circuits is experimentally scalable, but gives biased short-depth fidelity estimates because incomplete ensemble mixing introduces transient modes. Waiting for these transients to decay in deeper circuits can push the signal below the noise floor. This is a well-established obstacle, e.g. in linear cross-entropy benchmarking (LinXEB). Here we overcome this obstacle solely through classical post-processing. We introduce a one-parameter family of estimators that interpolate between the standard LinXEB-type post-processing and a new post-processing technique we call the trace filter function. Under practical assumptions, the trace filter function provably suppresses transient modes, exposing an interpretable fidelity decay at short depth, with theoretical guarantees comparable to standard RB, at the cost of an increased variance. We bound the variance, analyze the evaluation complexity of the new estimators, and develop practical post-processing algorithms. Experiments on a Rigetti superconducting processor validate the method for one-dimensional circuits of up to 12 qubits: where the standard estimator requires depth beyond a 40-layer experimental window, the trace filter function yields consistent estimates below 10 layers. Trace-filtered randomized benchmarking therefore extends reliable fidelity characterization to relevant structured circuit ensembles and short-depth regimes that are inaccessible to conventional estimators.
summary: This paper presents a new classical post-processing technique, the trace filter function, to overcome systematic biases in randomized benchmarking measurements. By suppressing transient decay modes, the method allows for accurate extraction of fidelity decay rates even when experimental circuits are too short for standard estimators to converge. This significantly extends the reliable characterization window for quantum hardware performance.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of obtaining accurate, unbiased estimates of fidelity decay rates from randomized benchmarking (RB) experiments when transient modes bias standard short-depth measurements.
main_result: A novel 'trace filter function' post-processing technique is introduced that provably suppresses these transient modes, enabling reliable fidelity characterization at circuit depths inaccessible to conventional estimators.
method: The authors develop and analyze a one-parameter family of estimators, culminating in the trace filter function, which is applied to the measured expectation values from random circuits.
model_or_system: The work is validated using experiments on a superconducting processor (Rigetti) for one-dimensional circuits up to 12 qubits, utilizing random Clifford circuits generated via brickwork patterns.
key_observables: Fidelity decay rate ($ eta$), transient modes, and the variance of the estimators.
important_parameters: The filter parameter $\alpha$, the circuit depth ($m$), and the qubit number ($n$).
main_assumptions: Assumptions include time-stationary Markovian gate-dependent noise and local-symmetry assumptions for the noise model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup (simulated and physical circuits), the comparison of different methods for determining the mixing length, and the theoretical scaling of moment calculations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the bias caused by transient modes in RB, introducing the interpolating estimator family, deriving the theoretical properties of the trace filter function (including its efficiency for local circuits), and validating the method with superconducting hardware experiments.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial algorithmic tool for characterizing decoherence in near-term quantum hardware, directly impacting the ability to benchmark quantum processors against theoretical limits.
